deep_why: The core task is adapting general-purpose conversation models to serve speakers of low-resource languages fairly. The underlying principle is that a language-agnostic model trained on high-resource data can be specialized through targeted prompting strategies that teach it language-specific patterns without full retraining. This works because modern models encode rich compositional structure—they can learn to follow instructions about how to shift their output toward different language characteristics once shown examples. For Tetun, where training data is sparse but the language structure exists, strategic prompts that ground the model in Tetun conventions act as guides that redirect the general-purpose weights toward language-faithful output. This approach extends access to AI services to marginalized communities by making customization practical without requiring thousands of hours of annotated speech.

The problem being solved is content homogenization: when systems chase statistical likelihood, they converge toward bland, repetitive text because the average is what occurs most in training data. The soundness principle is that strategic retrieval of relevant professional expertise followed by guided rewriting can shift the output distribution away from the mean toward distinctive, characteristic modes. By retrieving specific examples tied to a person's actual background and then prompting for distinctiveness, the system breaks the lock that generic probability-maximization creates. The reason this works for this person is that professional expertise, when explicitly retrieved and foregrounded, provides anchors that pull the output toward less-common but more authentic expressions. This lets individuals build genuine personal brands rather than indistinguishable AI-generated noise.

The problem is that interactive retrieval research is slow and throughput-limited when researchers must process many similar deep research tasks one at a time. The soundness principle is that identical workflows can be parallelized across independent instances if the system treats each research job as an isolated, schedulable unit with the same instruction set—like a processor executing the same operation on different data. This parallel execution improves throughput without losing the quality of individual reasoning because each instance still reasons through retrieval, synthesis, and verification independently. Deep research tasks have consistent structure (retrieve, read, verify, synthesize), so batching them is safe; what differs is only the content. This lets research teams scale from interactive one-by-one work to production pipelines that handle hundreds of papers with minimal latency per job.

The challenge is that information retrieval capabilities live in research tools while language models live in separate systems, making it hard to build retrieval-augmented systems. The soundness principle is establishing a standard interface (the Model Context Protocol) so that search, ranking, and evaluation tools can be called as actions by the language model, just like any other function. This works because standardization removes the friction of custom integration—tools expose their core operations as well-defined methods that the model can invoke to ground its reasoning in real evidence. Search and ranking are retrieval operations with clear inputs and outputs, so standardizing them as callable functions lets models benefit from specialized retrieval expertise without the tools needing to understand language generation. This bridges two communities and makes retrieval-augmented workflows practical for research and production use.

Peer review quality suffers when reviewers make claims that are subjective, rhetorical, or unsupported by the paper being reviewed. The system extracts check-worthy claims from reviews and then verifies them by retrieving manuscript evidence and applying logical inference—asking whether the claim follows from what the paper actually says. This works because claims are factual statements with truth conditions; if you can locate the relevant passage in the paper and reason about it, you can identify when a review makes unsupported assertions. The method is sound because it grounds verification in the primary source (the manuscript) rather than external knowledge, isolating the specific claim-evidence relationship that matters for fairness. By making verification rapid and visual, it enables program committees to detect unfair review statements at scale.

Video advertisement generation at scale fails when systems produce unreliable or factually incorrect outputs because they lack oversight of whether generated clips match real places. The system decomposes video creation into stages: planning themes, retrieving real anchor images of the destination, expanding those anchors into detailed prompts, and verifying the output for visual artifacts before assembly. This works because each stage grounds decisions in evidence external to the generation process itself—anchoring images are actual photographs, not guesses, and they constrain what plausible prompts can be. Verification before assembly catches artifacts before they reach users. By interleaving retrieval and verification throughout the agentic process rather than trusting a single generation pass, the system maintains factual coherence in travel advertising where users care whether ads show real places.

Complex queries on graphs often involve set-level constraints—finding groups of nodes with shared properties or relationships—but standard query systems optimize for single-node or simple-path operations. The system extends query language with monadic second-order logic, which lets users express set quantification directly, and implements a two-phase execution engine that avoids redundant evaluation of first-order conditions. This is sound because monadic logic's semantics are well-founded: asking whether a set of nodes satisfies a property has a clear true-or-false answer once the property is defined precisely. Reusing first-order clause results across multiple set-level queries avoids redundant work without changing correctness. The system's community-aware storage precomputes graph structure, exploiting the fact that meaningful subgraphs (communities) are usually stable. This lets practitioners express natural analytical questions about graph structure without low-level programming.

Museum collections span structured records, images, and unstructured text that museums struggle to integrate into a single queryable form. A knowledge graph unifies these by extracting entities and relations into a typed structure where objects, people, organizations, and images all have places and explicit links. This works because knowledge graphs organize information by identity and relationship rather than by source format—when you resolve all references to 'Creator A' to a single entity node regardless of whether they appeared in a catalog record or an image description, you enable exploration across sources. Natural-language queries can be grounded to these entities, and compact neighborhoods of the graph provide evidence for answers. The method is sound because it treats heterogeneous data as expressions of the same underlying entities and relations, making unified query and discovery possible.

Food recommenders often promote popular recipes, which tend to be less healthy, so users need explanations that help them understand and accept healthy trade-offs. The system generates personalized recipe recommendations and pairs them with natural-language explanations derived from nutritional data, then uses built-in A/B testing to measure whether explanations actually change user behavior toward healthier choices. This is sound because structured nutritional data can be translated into understandable language that shows users the reasoning behind recommendations, and controlled experiments reveal whether that transparency influences real decisions. The reason it works is that users who understand why a recommendation is healthy are more likely to try it, especially when the platform makes the explanation conspicuous. By combining algorithmic recommendation with transparent explanation and rigorous measurement, the system learns how to promote healthy eating through information design.

Scientists reading papers need related literature but manual searching interrupts their work and misses nuanced context about what they actually want to learn. The system builds a three-layered memory of the reader's background, the paper they're reading, and their implicit information needs, then proactively generates natural-language questions grounded in that context and retrieves relevant papers locally. This is sound because different readers have different information needs even for the same paper—an NLP specialist and an HCI specialist will ask different follow-up questions about the same work. By capturing reader background in memory and inferring implicit need from reading behavior, the system can generate profile-specific questions rather than generic ones. Local retrieval preserves privacy while preventing interruption; questions arise from the system's analysis, not manual entry. This lets scientists maintain reading flow while discovering relevant context.

Legal documents undergo frequent revision but character-level or token-level comparison tools miss paraphrases and semantic shifts—two phrasings that mean different things but look similar lexically. The system combines information retrieval techniques with language models to perform span-aware semantic comparison, moving beyond surface matching to meaning. This is sound because paraphrases are semantically equivalent, but semantic shifts change meaning; a system that reasons about meaning—not just character sequences—can distinguish them. Language models encode semantic understanding, so asking them to judge whether two spans mean the same thing after retrieving relevant context is more reliable than string matching. The reason this works is that legal documents are precise about meaning, and humans reviewing them need to spot where revisions inadvertently changed obligations, permissions, or constraints. Semantic comparison catches those shifts where syntactic diffs miss them.

Knowledge graphs like Wikidata are incomplete; link prediction can suggest missing relations, but predictions are unreliable without clear evidence. The system uses graph embeddings to generate candidate relations, retrieves Wikipedia passages to provide evidence, applies a language model to assess each candidate based on that evidence, and presents results for human validation. This is sound because predictions grounded in evidence are more trustworthy than predictions alone—when a human can read the evidence supporting a candidate link, they can verify whether it's correct before adding it to the graph. The reason this works is that reasoning about candidates given relevant passages is much faster and more reliable than reasoning about candidates in isolation. By making each step transparent and giving humans the evidence they need to validate, the system scales knowledge graph completion from slow manual work to rapid human-in-the-loop workflows.

Large language models generate long-form responses that may contain hallucinated facts, and evaluating factuality is slow and expensive with existing tools. FactOWL addresses this by extracting atomic facts from the response, retrieving supporting evidence from multiple Wikipedia sources and Wikidata triples, and aggregating across sources to handle ambiguity and incomplete contexts. This is sound because a fact's truth can be established through evidence from authoritative sources—if multiple sources support a claim, it's reliable; if none do, it's suspicious. Aggregating across multiple sources handles the problem that any single source may be incomplete or outdated. The reason multi-source aggregation works is that no single source is perfect, but consensus across sources is trustworthy. By using open, real-time data sources and efficient retrieval, the system makes factuality evaluation cheap and fast enough to be practical for researchers and applications.

Trademark clearance requires assessing whether a new mark might infringe existing registrations across visual, phonetic, and conceptual dimensions—a judgment task that ranked lists of candidates cannot solve alone because ranking finds candidates but doesn't judge them. The system retrieves candidates via multimodal search, then simulates an adversarial examination between an Examiner and an Applicant to reason through appearance, pronunciation, concept, and goods-and-services factors. This is sound because trademark judgment is grounded in examination practice, and simulating that practice reveals where conflicts arise. The Examiner-versus-Applicant exchange exposes reasoning about each dimension, producing risk scores that practitioners can review and refine. Re-simulating with adjusted inputs shows how outcomes change, enabling comparative judgment. This shifts the interface from ranked retrieval to reasoned comparative judgment, which is what trademark law actually requires.

Mathematics in PDFs is fragmented—symbols and text carry interdependent meaning, but standard PDF readers treat them separately and formula search tools live in isolation. MathMex-PDF detects and recognizes mathematical expressions, grounds them in document layout, and provides unified search over text and formulas using late-fusion retrieval that combines structure-aware formula matching with text embeddings and applies rank fusion. This is sound because mathematical meaning arises from both symbols and context, so searching them in isolation misses the semantic whole. Late fusion respects the different nature of formula and text retrieval (structural matching for formulas, dense similarity for text) while combining their results fairly. Grounding expressions in layout preserves the visual relationship between notation and surrounding explanation. By unifying these modalities and making the workflow accessible from a single reader, the system lets users explore mathematical content naturally without switching tools or losing context.
